newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK global trade gap to shrink in January.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK global trade gap to shrink in January.

text.p: Britain's trade deficit with the rest of the world is expected to have narrowed in January, economists said on Monday.
A Reuter poll of economists produced a consensus forecast that the trade gap would shrink to 760 million stg from 845 million in December.
"The improvement we expect in January is all due to the lower non-EU deficit already reported," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Figures for trade with non-European Union nations in January, released last month, showed Britain's trade shortfall dropped to 398 million stg from 640 million the month before.
February's non-EU figures will be released alongside January's global data at 0930 GMT on Wednesday. The non-EU trade gap is forecast to have ballooned back out to 580 million stg last month.
As has been the case for months now, economists have to tackle the problem of when the strong pound will start to squeeze export volumes, when compiling their trade forecasts.
So far, only the first half of the so-called "J-curve" effect has been seen -- a stronger currency cutting import prices and therefore improving trade figures in value terms.
With volumes slower to react to rising export prices it is only later that the terms of trade start to deteriorate.

"Once the illusory effects of the J-curve fall out later this year, the trade deficit should widen significantly," Barr said. He noted that import volume growth is already outstripping export volumes.
The pound has soared by about 15 percent on a trade-weighted basis since August last year.
But the full effect on volumes is likely to be delayed a while yet, economists said, and in value terms, import prices will fall further and continue to flatter Britain's trade performance.

Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, said import prices were down roughly five percent year-on-year in December but would probably drop between 10 to 15 percent on a year earlier in the months to come as the full extent of the pound's rally feeds through.

Whatever happens later this year, figures out on Monday showed Britain put in a surprisingly strong trade performance last year. It managed a current account surplus of 873 million pounds in the fourth quarter of last year, leaving a deficit of just 14 million on current account for 1996 as a whole.
Britain's booming service sector put in another storming performance, posting a record 1.94 billion stg surplus in the last quarter of the year.

"These are excellent figures showing the current account almost in balance," Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said. "They show that this time we have healthy growth which is not running into the balance of payments problems which caused past booms to turn into bust."

Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS, said the 1996 current account figure was the best since 1985. "The benficial value effect on these figures arising from sterling's recent appreciation is clearly outweighing any adverse effect on trade volumes at the moment."
